Dennis Rader: The BTK Serial Murder Case

Introduction

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:01
Instaread

“BTK” — short for “Bind, Torture, Kill” — was the acronym Dennis Lynn Rader adopted in his communications with law enforcement and the media to describe his violent impulses and methods. Rader became one of the most notorious serial killers in American history, evading detection for over three decades while taunting investigators through letters and packages. Before his capture, he was convicted of ten murders committed between 1974 and 1991 in and around Wichita, Kansas. In 2005, Rader was arrested, pleaded guilty to all ten counts of first-degree murder, and is serving ten consecutive life sentences at the El Dorado Correctional Facility in Kansas.

What is the BTK Case?

Between 1974 and 1991, the Wichita area was terrorized by an elusive serial killer. Dennis Rader began his murders in January 1974 when he targeted four members of the Otero family.

On January 15, 1974, Joseph Otero Sr. (38), Julia Maria “Julie” Otero (33), Joseph Otero II “Joey” (9), and Josephine “Josie” Otero (11) were found dead inside their Wichita home. Rader confessed that he entered the home, held the family hostage at gunpoint, and bound them. He suffocated Joseph, Julie, and Joey, and hanged Josie from a pipe in the basement. Semen was recovered from the basement crime scene. In October 1974, Rader left a letter inside an engineering textbook at the Wichita Public Library claiming responsibility, writing: “The code words for me will be… Bind them, torture them, kill them, B.T.K.”

On April 4, 1974, Rader broke into the home of 21-year-old Kathryn Bright. When Kathryn and her 19-year-old brother, Kevin Bright, returned home, Rader held them at gunpoint and forced Kevin to tie up his sister. Rader shot Kevin in the head and attempted to strangle Kathryn. When he was unable to subdue her by strangulation, he stabbed her. Kevin survived his injuries and escaped to seek help; Kathryn later died from her wounds at the hospital.

After a three-year hiatus, Rader struck again on March 17, 1977, targeting 24-year-old Shirley Vian (often recorded as Shirley Vian Relford). He held her three young children at gunpoint and locked them in the bathroom. He then tied Vian to the bed, placed a plastic bag over her head, and strangled her with a rope. The children managed to escape through a window to summon help.

On December 8, 1977, Rader stalked and entered the home of 25-year-old Nancy Fox, strangling her with a belt in her bedroom. Following the murder, Rader placed a call to police from a public payphone to report the location of Fox’s body.

Irritated by the lack of sustained media coverage following the Fox homicide, Rader sent a letter and poem to KAKE-TV in early 1978, asking: “How many do I have to kill before I get a name in the paper or some national attention?”

In April 1985, Rader killed his neighbor, 53-year-old Marine Wallace Hedge. He entered her residence, strangled her, transported her body to Christ Lutheran Church, where he served as president of the congregation council, photographed her body in bondage poses, and later disposed of it in a rural ditch.

On September 16, 1986, Rader broke into the residence of 28-year-old Vicki Wegerle, strangling her with a nylon stocking. On January 19, 1991, Rader targeted 62-year-old Dolores E. Davis, abducting her from her home and strangling her. Her body was found 13 days later beneath a bridge. Following the 1991 murder, Rader remained dormant for over a decade.

Rader’s Arrest

In 2004, media coverage marking the 30th anniversary of the Otero murders revived public attention to the unsolved BTK case. Rader subsequently resurfaced and began communicating with police and the media, sending letters, packages, photographs and personal items taken from victims, some of which were concealed in cereal boxes or left at designated locations.

Rader asked police whether he could communicate with them using a floppy disk without being traced. Investigators responded through a classified advertisement in The Wichita Eagle stating: “Rex, it will be OK.” On February 16, 2005, Rader mailed a purple 1.44 MB Memorex floppy disk to KSAS-TV.

Forensic examiners recovered a deleted Microsoft Word document from the disk. Its metadata showed that the document had been last modified by a user identified as “Dennis” and was associated with “Christ Lutheran Church.” Investigators conducted an Internet search for the church and discovered that Dennis Rader was its congregation council president.

Science

Investigators subsequently obtained a warrant for a medical sample from Rader’s daughter. DNA testing produced a familial match between the sample and biological evidence associated with the Wegerle investigation, providing additional evidence linking Rader to the crimes.

On February 25, 2005, law enforcement conducted a traffic stop and arrested Rader near his home in Park City. Searches of his home, church, and workplace uncovered physical and documentary evidence linking him to the crimes, including victim souvenirs and photographs. After his arrest, Rader confessed to the murders and provided investigators with detailed information regarding the crimes and the locations of additional evidence.

Because Kansas had no death penalty in effect when Rader committed the murders, prosecutors could not seek a death sentence for these crimes. Rader was sentenced to ten consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole for 175 years.

Law Enforcement

Rader’s Background

Dennis Lynn Rader was born on March 9, 1945, in Pittsburg, Kansas, the eldest of four sons born to Dorothea Mae Rader and William Elvin Rader. He married Paula Dietz in 1971, with whom he had two children, Kerri and Brian.

Rader later described developing sadistic sexual fantasies involving bondage and control during his youth. He also reported engaging in voyeurism, autoerotic asphyxiation, and cruelty toward animals. Despite these private compulsions, Rader maintained an outward image of civic respectability. He served in the U.S. Air Force from 1966 to 1970, served as a Cub Scout leader, and was elected president of the church council at Christ Lutheran Church.

He worked as an assembler at the Coleman Company from 1972 to 1973 and briefly worked for Cessna Aircraft before joining ADT Security Services in November 1974. He installed home security systems at ADT until July 1988. After leaving ADT in 1988, he worked for the U.S. Census Bureau before becoming a compliance officer and animal-control officer for Park City in 1991.

Where is the BTK Killer?

Rader is incarcerated at the El Dorado Correctional Facility in Kansas. Post-arrest psychological assessments reported narcissistic, antisocial, and obsessive-compulsive personality pathology.

References

  • Douglas, John E., and Johnny Dodd. Inside the Mind of BTK: The True Story Behind the Thirty-Year Hunt for the Notorious Wichita Serial Killer. Jossey-Bass, 2007.
  • Wenzl, Roy, Tim Potter, Hurst Laviana, and L. Kelly. Bind, Torture, Kill: The Inside Story of BTK, the Serial Killer Next Door. William Morrow, 2007.
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation. Dennis Rader (BTK). FBI Records: The Vault.
  • State of Kansas v. Dennis L. Rader, Case No. 05-CR-498 (18th Jud. Dist. Ct., Sedgwick County, Kan. 2005) (Plea and Sentencing Transcripts).
